jurisdiction: United States (federal and state law). The lesson states this scope explicitly because 'public education' is otherwise ambiguous across countries.

core: Public education in the United States as a state responsibility exercised through local districts, with a conditional federal role
The common school movement of the 1830s-1850s and Horace Mann's tenure as first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education
Compulsory attendance laws: Massachusetts 1852 through the last state in 1918, and the gap between enactment and enforcement
The expansion of secondary schooling from a minority experience to a near-universal one

Exclusion and segregation as part of the system's construction: Plessy (1896), the federal Indian boarding school system, Mendez (1946-47), Brown (1954-55), Plyler (1982), and the pre-1975 exclusion of children with disabilities
Federal involvement through ESEA (1965), EHA/IDEA (1975, 1990, 2004), NCLB (2002), and ESSA (2015)
The standing tension between local control, state responsibility, and federal leverage
Distinguishing event, evidence, and interpretation, including genuine historiographical disagreement about why common schooling spread
supporting: Colonial precedents (Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1642) as a legal ancestor rather than a direct origin of public schooling
Freedmen's Bureau (established 1865) support for schools during Reconstruction
Current federal, state, and local shares of public school revenue
Cooper v. Aaron (1958) as evidence that Brown required enforcement, not just declaration
outOfScope: Higher education history and land-grant colleges
Contemporary policy debates over vouchers, charters, and curriculum content
Any individualized legal advice about a reader's own school, district, or child

claims.claim: Education in the United States is primarily a state and local responsibility; states and communities establish schools, set curricula, and set graduation requirements, and the federal government supplies a minority of funding.

The U.S. Department of Education states that the federal government contributes about 8 percent of funding for elementary and secondary education across all federal agencies; NCES reports that in school year 2020-21, 11 percent of public school revenues came from federal sources, 46 percent from state sources, and 44 percent from local sources.
claims.status: supported with a recorded conflict; the lesson gives the range and its cause rather than a single number

claims.claim: Massachusetts created a state Board of Education by an act dated April 20, 1837 titled 'An Act Relating to Common Schools'; Horace Mann became its first secretary and served until he left for Congress in 1848. The board was given duties of information-gathering and persuasion rather than direct power over towns.

The first U.S. state compulsory school attendance law was Massachusetts Acts of 1852, chapter 240, 'An Act concerning the Attendance of Children at School,' approved by the Governor on May 18, 1852. It required a person controlling a child aged eight to fourteen to send the child to a public school in the town or city of residence for at least twelve weeks per year, six of them consecutive.
claims.status: supported by the primary statutory text

claims.claim: The 1852 Massachusetts act carried a penalty of not more than twenty dollars, assigned inquiry to the town or city school committee and prosecution to the treasurer, and exempted children schooled elsewhere, children who had already acquired the branches taught in common schools, children prevented by bodily or mental condition, and families unable to comply by reason of poverty.
claims.status: supported by the primary statutory text

claims.claim: Compulsory attendance requirements spread state by state: about thirty-two states had adopted them by 1900, and in 1918 Mississippi became the last state then in the Union to enact one.
Enactment of compulsory attendance laws preceded effective enforcement; many states were unsuccessful at enforcing them until the 1930s.

Secondary schooling expanded from a minority experience to a near-universal one: U.S. high school graduates as a ratio of the 17-year-old population were 2.0 percent in 1869-70, 6.4 percent in 1899-1900, 16.8 percent in 1919-20, 50.8 percent in 1939-40, 69.5 percent in 1959-60, and 87.9 percent in 2021-22.

In Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537, decided May 18, 1896, the Supreme Court upheld an 1890 Louisiana law requiring separate railway accommodations by race, by a vote of 7-1 with Justice Harlan dissenting, establishing the 'separate but equal' doctrine.

In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483, decided May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court held that separating children in public schools by race violates the Equal Protection Clause and that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, rejecting Plessy's doctrine in public education. On May 31, 1955, in a follow-up decision, the Court directed desegregation to proceed 'with all deliberate speed.'
Brown required continued enforcement: in Cooper v. Aaron, 358 U.S. 1 (1958), the Supreme Court held that states could not use state authority to obstruct desegregation.

In Mendez v. Westminster, U.S. District Judge Paul J. McCormick ruled in February 1946 that segregating children of Mexican descent in Orange County, California school districts violated the Fourteenth Amendment; the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed in 1947 (Westminster School Dist. v. Mendez, 161 F.2d 774), and California then became the first state to repeal its school segregation statutes. The NAACP brief in Mendez was authored by Robert Carter, Thurgood Marshall, and Loren Miller and anticipated arguments used in Brown.
claims.status: supported; see conflictingEvidence on the appellate date

claims.claim: In Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202 (1982), the Supreme Court held that denying free public education to undocumented children violates the Equal Protection Clause.

The Department of the Interior's Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative identified 417 federal Indian boarding schools across 37 states or then-territories, documented federal appropriations for the system between 1871 and 1969, confirmed at least 973 documented deaths of American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian children at these schools, and identified at least 74 marked and unmarked burial sites at 65 school sites. The Department describes the policies as deliberate efforts to separate children from families and suppress their languages and cultures.
The Freedmen's Bureau was established within the War Department by act of Congress on March 3, 1865, and assisted benevolent societies in establishing schools for formerly enslaved people.

President Johnson signed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act on April 11, 1965 in Johnson City, Texas; the law directed grants to districts serving low-income students and support for instructional materials and state and local education agencies.

The Education for All Handicapped Children Act (Public Law 94-142) was signed on November 29, 1975 by President Ford, guaranteeing a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment with the individualized education program as the primary vehicle; the statute was renamed the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1990 and reauthorized in 2004. Before the law, roughly 1.8 million children with disabilities were excluded from public schools; more than 8 million were served under IDEA in school year 2022-23.
The Every Student Succeeds Act, signed December 10, 2015, reauthorized the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 and replaced the No Child Left Behind Act, which had been enacted in 2002.

Historians genuinely disagree about why common schooling spread. A liberal or consensus interpretation associated with Lawrence Cremin treats it as a democratic achievement; a revisionist interpretation associated with Michael B. Katz's The Irony of Early School Reform and Bowles and Gintis's Schooling in Capitalist America treats it as social control and reproduction of inequality; later work by Carl Kaestle, David Tyack, and James Anderson complicates both.
claims.status: supported as a description of the historiographical debate; the lesson presents it as disagreement, not as a settled finding

claims.claim: The first compulsory education law in what became the United States was enacted in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1642, which is a legal ancestor of compulsory attendance rather than the beginning of tax-supported public schooling.

positions: U.S. Department of Education: the federal government contributes about 8 percent of elementary and secondary education funding across all federal agencies.

NCES Condition of Education: 11 percent of public school revenues in school year 2020-21 came from federal sources; other NCES reporting puts the 2021-22 federal share near 10.7 percent, elevated by pandemic relief funds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states a range (roughly 8-11 percent depending on year and accounting) and names pandemic relief as the reason recent years run high, rather than asserting one figure as the permanent number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Date the Ninth Circuit affirmed Mendez
positions: A National Park Service article describes the Ninth Circuit as upholding Judge McCormick's decision in late 1946.
The published reporter citation is Westminster School Dist. of Orange County v. Mendez, 161 F.2d 774 (9th Cir. 1947), and multiple accounts date the affirmance to April 14, 1947.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the reporter year: district court ruling in 1946, affirmance in 1947. It does not assert a specific day, since the day was not confirmed against the opinion itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Motives behind the common school movement
positions: Consensus/liberal historiography (Cremin, Bailyn): common schooling as an extension of democratic and religious commitments to literacy and civic participation.
Revisionist historiography (Michael B. Katz, Bowles and Gintis): common schooling as social control, bureaucratic ordering, and reproduction of class position.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented in the lesson as an unresolved interpretive disagreement, with the observation that both sides mostly agree on the documentary record and disagree about what it means.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing historical at all: it described 'History Of Public Education' as a generic concept with placeholder text about defining a term, identifying its limits, and applying it to a scenario. None of that was supported by, or even about, the history of U.S. public education.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined the topic circularly as 'a foundational Education concept covered in this lesson.'
The draft's quick-check items tested generic study skills rather than any historical or legal content, and carried three options rather than four.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with a sourced U.S.-specific history, stating jurisdiction explicitly.
Added dates, statutory citations, and case citations verified against primary statutory text, National Archives, federal judiciary, ED, NCES, DOI, and NPS sources.
Integrated exclusion and segregation into the main narrative rather than treating it as an addendum.
Separated event, evidence, and interpretation, and represented the historiographical disagreement about common schooling instead of choosing a side.
Rebuilt the question bank as five four-option items with explanations, difficulty, skill, and source ids.
rightsIssues: No source prose was reproduced. Short factual figures (dates, citations, counts, percentages) are used as facts, not as expression.
The 1852 Massachusetts statute and the 1898 Hinsdale biography are old enough to be in the public domain in the United States; the lesson still paraphrases rather than quoting at length.

Federal agency pages (ED, NCES, NARA, NPS, DOI, U.S. Courts) and the Duke, ERIC, LBJ Library, and Syracuse items are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY because their reuse terms were not individually verified for this project.
AI-ingestion permissions were not individually verified for any source; recorded as unchecked and treated conservatively.
No quotation was invented. Where a source's characterization is used (for example Hinsdale's assessment of the 1837 Massachusetts board), the lesson attributes it as that author's judgment.
